tagline: The largest animal that has ever lived
summary: A slender, mottled blue-grey rorqual that can pass 30 metres and 150 tonnes, making it the largest animal known to have existed. It lives almost entirely on krill, gulping huge mouthfuls of water and straining them through baleen, and its low, powerful calls carry across ocean basins.
ability: lunge feeding: engulfing and filtering vast mouthfuls of krill

stats.size: Up to about 33 m and 150 tonnes in the Antarctic; about 27 m in the North Atlantic and North Pacific
stats.depth: Feeds in the upper ocean; tagged whales dived to 204 m
stats.range: All oceans except the Arctic; summers on polar feeding grounds, winters towards the tropics
stats.diet: Almost exclusively krill; occasionally fish and copepods

facts.title: Bigger than any dinosaur
facts.text: NOAA describes the blue whale as the largest animal ever to live on our planet. Antarctic blue whales are the biggest, reaching about 33 m and more than 150 tonnes; females are generally larger than males.

facts.title: A mouthful of krill
facts.text: It swims at a swarm of krill with its mouth open, inflating its pleated throat, then pushes the water out with its tongue while baleen plates hanging from the roof of the mouth hold the krill inside. The biggest whales may eat around 5 tonnes of krill a day.

facts.title: Two beats a minute
facts.text: An electrocardiogram tag on a whale feeding in Monterey Bay recorded heart rates of 4–8 beats a minute during dives, and as low as 2. Back at the surface the heart raced at 25–37 beats a minute.

facts.title: Short, shallow dives
facts.text: For such a big animal it does not dive for long. Seven tagged blue whales off California reached at most 204 m, and their longest dive lasted 14.7 minutes.

facts.title: Songs that are dropping in pitch
facts.text: Recordings going back to the 1960s show that blue whale songs worldwide are slowly getting lower. The song heard off California is now sung about 31% lower than in the 1960s, and no single explanation has been proved.

facts.title: Age written in earwax
facts.text: Scientists estimate a whale's age by counting the layers in the waxy earplugs of dead animals. On that basis blue whales are thought to live for around 80 to 90 years.

notes: Taxonomy, order (Cetartiodactyla) and AphiaID from the WoRMS REST API. IUCN status: the IUCN site blocks scripts, so the 2018 assessment (Cooke; errata 2019) was confirmed via its DOI on Crossref, GBIF's IUCN category (EN) and the IUCN SSC Cetacean Specialist Group status page; subspecies and subpopulations have their own listings. NOAA gives size in feet/pounds and krill in US tons; converted (110 ft ≈ 33.5 m, 330,000 lb ≈ 150 t, 6 tons ≈ 5.4 t). Depth gauge uses Croll et al. (2001): maximum dive 204 m among seven tagged whales; Goldbogen et al. (2019) recorded dives to 184 m. Deeper dives may occur but no better-sourced maximum was found. Hero (anim1754) is a NOAA Photo Library image identified as Balaenoptera musculus; location and photographer not given. Regions exclude the Arctic Ocean, following NOAA.
